title: Revisiting Spolsky's "Things You Should Never Do, Part I"
summary: Natasha Jaffe revisits Spolsky with three rewrites and one refactor from her career: rewrites can succeed when the code is small, the product is not the breadwinner and the business case is strong; otherwise refactor in place.

assertions.quote: If this goes on for long enough your competitors will eat your lunch.
Old code is hairy for a reason. Each one of those hairs represents a weird bug that was detected, fixed, and vetted in real life.
If the business case is strong then think critically about the size and complexity of the code as it stands today.

verdicts.note: Derived from a handful of personal cases; plausible conditions with no broader data.

assertions.quote: accurately estimating the time a rewrite will take is very hard

verdicts.note: Consistent with overrun data showing large projects overrun most, though the exponential form is hand-waved.

Larger tasks are underestimated more (magnitude bias) in controlled experiments, but the observational link between project size and overrun is partly a statistical artefact and the authors do not know how much it applies to large projects.

assertions.quote: at least with a refactor you get to deliver value along the way and stay alive
If your only reason for completely rewriting your codebase is tech debt and visceral ick, don't do it.

verdicts.note: Consistent with Spolsky and with rewrite failure cases; opinion-based.
